headlines.article_text: Palo Alto Networks (PANW) Q1 2027 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Palo Alto Networks topped Wall Street's fiscal first-quarter estimates. The company is buying AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. Fears of AI-led attacks have fueled demand for Palo Alto's tools. In this article PANW Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:22 02:22 Palo Alto shares pop on Q1 revenue and earnings beat, raises full-year guidance Closing Bell: Overtime Palo Alto Networks shares jumped more than 7% after the cybersecurity firm beat Wall Street's fiscal first quarter estimates and inked a deal for artificial intelligence startup Applied Compute . Here's how the company did versus LSEG estimates: Earnings per share : $1.05 adjusted vs. 97 cents expected Revenue : $3.44 billion vs $3.31 billion expected Revenue jumped 39% from $2.47 billion in the year-ago quarter. Fears of AI-powered cyberattacks, heightened by incidents like the Hugging Face breach, are driving demand for cybersecurity vendors like Palo Alto Networks. Amid this backdrop, shares have jumped 85% this year. "As AI reshapes the threat landscape, we must continually evolve to protect our customers and enable them to adopt AI securely," CEO Nikesh Arora said in a release. Palo Alto said annual recurring revenue for its next-generation security business jumped 66% from a year ago to $9.73 billion. Arora said the NGS ARR was one of the highest beats in the company's history. The cybersecurity company bumped up guidance for fiscal year 2027 as business spend more on security in the age of AI. Palo Alto expects adjusted earnings per share in the range of $4.26 to 4.30 and revenue in the range of $14.52 billion to 14.57 billion. The forecasts topped the earnings of $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion in revenue expected by analysts. Net income totaled $482 million, or 57 cents per share, up from $334 million, or 47 cents per share, a year ago. Palo Alto Networks has been steadily acquiring companies to capitalize on demand for cyber tools in the age of AI. Arora said the company's $4.5 billion all-stock deal for Applied Compute will help businesses secure open-weight models as adoption grows. The startup helps businesses run and customize their own AI models and marks a major investment for Palo Alto beyond cybersecurity. "If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity," Arora said on an earnings call. "This could be bigger than what we do." Outages from Microsoft, banks and the FAA have heightened concerns around cyberattacks over the last week. U.S. officials have so far ruled out any malicious activity, but experts say the rapid acceleration in patching is straining dated systems. As businesses discover more vulnerabilities, Arora said the company expects tens of thousands of virtual patches by the end of the fiscal year. "Whatever they do today is going to take three to six months, maybe nine months, depending on how complex and how tired their environment is," Arora said. Palo Alto Networks stock chart. headlines.article_text: Dealbook Summit 2026: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Andrew Ross Sorkin speaks onstage during The New York Times DealBook Summit 2025 at Jazz at Lincoln Center, Dec. 3, 2025 in New York City. David Dee Delgado | Getty Images Artificial intelligence, trade tensions, and the need to create trust have been recurring themes at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Andrew Ross Sorkin , founder and editor of DealBook and co-anchor of CNBC's "Squawk Box," has been sitting down in New York with prominent business, economic and political leaders to discuss a wide range of newsmaking issues. The conference comes as OpenAI rival Anthropic is about to make its public debut on Thursday, and it follows a series of widespread tech outages that have grounded airplanes, snarled email, and stymied banking transactions, among other disruptions — a dramatic reminder of society's dependency on these services. In discussing the balancing act that tech leaders are confronting trying to push ahead with AI innovation while attempting to guarantee public safety, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said, "The race dynamic in the fog of war, I think, is a bad thing. I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted." Skydance co-CEO David Ellison emphasized the need to rebuild trust in media organizations. "In a world, you know, where very quickly you're not going to be able to believe your eyes, we think having institutions that earn trust every single day is incredibly important," he said. Meanwhile, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed some frustration over trade relations with the U.S. He said a new deal "should have been done six months ago, but we're not going to sign something that doesn't make sense for Canada." He said he's pressing on in forging other trade partnerships. "We got a lot to do, so we would like to do the deal. But if the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy," he said. Highlights from the DealBook Summit include: Altman and Brockman have personally reached out to Jensen Huang following his ouster Canada PM Mark Carney 'can't unsee' how Starlink became 'a vulnerability' to Ukraine Ellison: Larry Ellison 'demands an incredible performance' Luckey says U.S. needs to bring back nuclear weapons tests New York Mayor Mamdani says midterms showed Americans want 'new kind of politics' 9 Min Ago Microsoft CEO Nadella says he is 'extremely sorry' for extended Outlook outage Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella speaks during the 2026 DealBook Summit in the Appel Room at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. Spencer Platt | Getty Images Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was "extremely sorry" to those affected by the company's Outlook email software outage that played out over almost 24 hours last week. "This was a latent bug that was there; it got invoked, and you know, it's one of those perfect storms," Nadella told Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook Summit. "We put out an incident response, and we're going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural as well as operational, and fix that." Nadella used the occasion to talk about making software resilient to cybersecurity risks. Thanks to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, Microsoft now has more capable technology to find software vulnerabilities, and patching them rapidly is critical to prevent exploits, Nadella said. There are new three critical updates for open-source software, he said. "Then simultaneously we have this other thing where the floor of cyber attacks has fallen, right?" he said. "Because you now have essentially, whether with these AI models, someone can send a Telegram message to this Artex harness in the cloud somewhere, and then you have essentially a nation-state level persistent attacker going after you all the time. So, so that means we have a lot of fragility, and we have to deal with it." — Jordan Novet 35 Min Ago Mamdani doesn't think California's defeat of billionaire tax means idea is DOA New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (R) speaks with New York Times financial columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin during the 2026 DealBook Summit in the Appel Room at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. Spencer Platt | Getty Images New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he doesn't think the defeat of a "billionaire's tax" referendum in California means that the idea is doomed to fail elsewhere. There were "three other ballot referendums that took place across the country, calling for what is essentially the same thing, which is higher taxes on the wealthiest, and those all passed," Mamdani said. "And I also think what we saw in that referendum, though, from a vantage point of many, many miles away, is an incredible amount of spending in opposition to it," the mayor said. — Dan Mangan 51 Min Ago Mamdani says that despite Trump 'bromance' he'd still call president a 'fascist' New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during the 2026 DealBook Summit in the Appel Room at Lincoln Center on Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. Spencer Platt | Getty Images New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that despite people saying he has a "bromance" with President Donald Trump, he would still call him a "fascist," as he has previously — but also said Trump gets New York. Mamdani demurred when asked if Trump — who had called Mamdani a "communist" had ever raised the fact that the mayor used the "F" word about him. "I'll keep the conversations between the president and myself private," Mamdani said. "But I will tell you that we both know how we feel about the other's policies, and we both love the same city." "Usually, when you're calling someone at a national level, they might not be as familiar with the intricacies of New York City," the mayor said. "The president is very familiar. I do not have to explain what a bodega is to the president. "He's also the most famous developer the city has ever seen, and I'm also not shy about the places in which we have serious disagreement, because I think that it is incumbent upon us in elected office to be honest about those places of disagreement and also have these conversations so long as they can deliver for the people of the city," the mayor said. — Dan Mangan 58 Min Ago New York Mayor Mamdani says midterms showed Americans want 'new kind of politics' New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani appears backstage during the NY Times Dealbook Summit at Jazz at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. "In [Texas Sen.-elect] James Talarico, you see a call for universal pre-K, and [Georgia Gov.-elect] Keisha Lance Bottoms, you are seeing the importance of streamlining affordable housing production. If you're looking at Michigan's governor's race, you're seeing a data moratorium." "These are the kinds of things that have motivated many to not just repudiate federal policies that have made their lives more expensive, but also to call for a different kind of approach in what politics can actually deliver to working people's lives," Mamdani said. — Dan Mangan 1 Hour Ago Nasdaq CEO says the exchange is developing 'guardrails' as it heads toward 23/5 trading in December Adena Friedman speaks onstage during the NY Times Dealbook Summit at Jazz at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. headlines.article_text: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, above expected range, source tells CNBC Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, a person familiar told CNBC, above the expected range. The AI company is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" on Thursday. Should the company sell all 825 million shares it had originally planned for the offering, the IPO will raise about $68.5 billion. In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei speaks during INBOUND 2025 Powered by HubSpot at Moscone Center in San Francisco, Sept. 4, 2025. Chance Yeh | Getty Images Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, a person familiar told CNBC, above the expected range, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing and a historic moment for the artificial intelligence industry. The company previously said it was offering 825 million shares. If that number holds and all of shares are sold at the IPO price, Anthropic would raise roughly $68.5 billion. Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record, raising $75 billion initially and a total of $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their overallotment. Anthropic's market cap will depend on total shares outstanding, but the share price would put the valuation above the $1.4 trillion that Anthropic was previously targeting. The stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT." The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. After publicly unveiling its prospectus in October, Anthropic updated the document last week with an expected price range between $70 and $78 per share. Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD. What this analyst expects from the AI giant Anthropic IPO is not important anymore: 'Big Short' investor Steve Eisman Altimeter's Brad Gerstner aims to invest $5 billion in Anthropic IPO Anthropic IPO guide: Everything you need to know Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic Anthropic's Wall Street whisperer: CFO Krishna Rao "I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time." Amodei co-founded Anthropic in 2021 alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO. "Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort." headlines.article_text: Nvidia sinks after earnings, dragging down neoclouds CoreWeave, Iren Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Nvidia beat on earnings and revenue Tuesday after the bell. The chip giant's earnings came at a tumultuous time for the company, following former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation last week. Chair of the board Harvey Jones said on the earnings call Huang would not return as CEO. In this article NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:32 01:32 Nvidia interim CEO dismisses exodus fears after Huang’s exit, citing ‘high confidence’ in the team Mad Money with Jim Cramer Nvidia shares declined another 2.89% Wednesday after the company issued its first earnings report since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang . The stock is down more than 13% over the past week. Trading in the neocloud companies was volatile throughout the day, as CoreWeave closed down 4.13%, Iren sank 3.61% and Nebius whipsawed, ending the trading day up 0.87%. Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG. The semiconductor giant continues to navigate the fallout from Huang's resignation last week. Shortly before the results, Huang made his first public statement since resigning last week, saying that he was open to returning to the company, after an outpouring of support from prominent tech figures . Neocloud stocks today But Harvey Jones, the new and first-ever chair of Nvidia's board, said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. ″[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," interim CEO Colette Kress told Jim Cramer on CNBC's "Mad Money." "This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers." The U.S. Commerce Department announced a legal change on Monday to try and stem China's access to the most advanced Nvidia chips — which are already under export controls effectively preventing their import into the country — by restricting Chinese companies' ability to access compute remotely in overseas data centers. In a letter Wednesday, the House Energy and Commerce Committee asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear to discuss chip export controls, and requested a briefing from interim CEO Colette Kress by Dec. 2. Nvidia told investors in its earnings commentary that it was "not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook," in keeping with its recent language on the country. Huang is slated to appear before several Congressional committees in the coming weeks. Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday, Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Huang and Lutnick have agreed to appear before the committee in December. It's slated to be Huang's second appearance on Capitol Hill in December, after the former Nvidia CEO reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for closed-door interviews on Dec. 1.
